## June 23, 1956

You arrived on a Saturday, into the hottest summer of the American century's second act.

---

**You share a birthday with Alan Turing.** The mathematician who conceived of the modern computer, broke the Nazi Enigma code, and first asked whether machines could think was born on June 23, 1912 — exactly 44 years before you. Turing had died just two years earlier, in June 1954, convicted of "gross indecency" for his homosexuality and chemically castrated by the British government that once depended on him to win the war. He was 41. On the day you were born, he was two years gone, largely uncelebrated, his wartime contributions still classified. You would live to see him pardoned, lionized, placed on the British fifty-pound note, and recognized as the intellectual godfather of the artificial intelligence now reshaping the world at age 70. The arc from his birth to your lifetime is the entire arc of the computer age.

**The Montgomery Bus Boycott was already six months in.** Rosa Parks had refused to give up her seat in December 1955. When you arrived, the boycott — 40,000 Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama walking miles to work every day — had been running half a year with no end in sight. It would continue until December 1956, when the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional. You were born mid-struggle, into a country actively contesting who counted as fully human within it. The civil rights decade that followed would be the defining moral drama of your childhood.

**Rock and roll was exploding in real time.** Elvis Presley's "Heartbreak Hotel" had gone to number one in April. "Hound Dog" would arrive in July. Ed Sullivan would book Elvis in September, and the country would never be the same. You were born into the exact season when popular music cracked open and something new — louder, sexier, more electric — poured through. Your entire generation would grow up inside what that rupture made possible.

**Six days after your birth, America built its roads.** On June 29, 1956 — one week after you arrived — President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, authorizing 41,000 miles of interstate highways. The single largest public works project in American history, it would reshape where people lived, how cities grew, what suburbs became, and how deeply the automobile embedded itself in national identity. You grew up in the country that act built.

**The Cold War was reinventing itself.** In February 1956, four months before your birth, Nikita Khrushchev had given his "Secret Speech" to the Soviet Communist Party — a stunning denunciation of Stalin's crimes that leaked almost immediately to the West. It shattered the myth of Soviet infallibility and set off revolts across the Eastern Bloc. By October 1956, the Hungarian Revolution was crushed by Soviet tanks, and the Suez Crisis exposed the terminal decline of British imperial power. You entered a world whose power structures were publicly cracking even as they tried to hold.

---

**The lifetime arc.** You turned 7 the year Kennedy was shot. You were 12 when both Martin Luther King and Robert Kennedy were killed within two months of each other, when cities burned and the Democratic convention became a street battle. At 13 you watched Neil Armstrong walk on the moon on a grainy television screen. You were 33 when the Berlin Wall came down and the Cold War ended — not with the nuclear catastrophe your childhood prepared you for, but with crowds chipping at concrete with hammers. You were 45 on September 11, 2001. You were 64 when COVID closed the world.

Now 70, you've lived to see the Turing question — *can machines think?* — answered, at least partially, in ways that are still being absorbed. The man whose birthday you share died wondering. You're watching it unfold.

---

You were born into American confidence — postwar prosperity, new highways, televisions in every living room, a country that had won the war and was building a future that felt inevitable. What followed was anything but. Civil rights, assassinations, Vietnam, Watergate, stagflation, AIDS, the internet, 9/11, a pandemic, and now the machines. Each decade handed something the previous one would have called impossible, catastrophic, or miraculous. Sometimes all three at once. That is the particular education of a life begun on June 23, 1956.
